speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This conversation with John Sanderson took place at his home near Bovill on July 25, 1975. The interviewer is Sam Schrager.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: After that I went to Grangeville and I had a picture gallery over there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's right… you used to be a photographer, didn't you?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: I got lots of plates in there now. The old pictures.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were you born in Palouse?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No… i was born in Iowa in P Harry III, just the beginning of the year. Then at four years old, Dad and Mother came west.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Why did they decide to come out here?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Father was always a man that was wanting to get someplace else. He wanted to come west. He had been running a cordless engine for the warehouses in Cloquet, Minnesota. He had a friend out here, Henry Hoskins, and he had a little sawmill. That was putting yards in the sawmill. They operated that mill for several years. It went down to Kendrick. Finally it moved from down near Potlatch to Kendrick.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was the mill at Palouse to start with?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No, it wasn't.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You know where Potlatch is?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, it was about three or four miles from Potlatch. That creek that goes in on the south side of the river, Rock Creek. They had a mill back in there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember Cloquet at all?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Oh, a little bit, not much.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember the trip out here? What was that like for a little kid?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, it was interesting on the train. It was about three or four days on the train. The folks didn't have a sleeper. They slept in the seats. They would transfer the seats to kind of a bed and lay down. There was three or four days coming to Spokane… they crossed Montana… to me it seemed like a long time at that age. But I guess it was only three or four days.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What was the Potlatch area like then when you first got there?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, Potlatch didn't start until about twelve, I think. The old building area had discovered this body of white wine. He couldn't read and write. He was just a lumberjack. He went to Weyerhaeuser… he said, Weyerhaeuser… i know Weyerhaeuser had finished up at Teakean and was wanting to get movies, mills, and stock business again. He really had taken the timber off of the... Iron Range. He lost more money by losing the Iron Range than they'd taken off on timber. So Bill went to him and he told him, he says, Weyerhaeuser, I know where there is a bunch of white wine timber, a big bunch. Something that you can buy reasonably. But he says, I'm going to tell you something. I'm not telling you where it is until I am sure that I'm put in on it. Well, Weyerhaeuser says, if you can put me into a good bunch of white wine timber, I'll see that you'll get your part. Well, Bill says, All right. He brought him up here and showed him this white wine timber. It was a big bunch, a good many million feet.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Weyerhaeuser was impressed. He liked it. He felt pretty good.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: They went to Boise and Weyerhaeuser bought it for a song. He made it, put it in the mills at Potlatch. He made a amount of money out of this. But in a few years, the timber went a good deal more stumpage than he got and saw lumber. But that was a pretty big male project that he put in at Potlatch at that time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember what your father thought about Weyerhaeuser coming into this country? He'd already worked for Weyerhaeuser back in the Midwest. What did he think of him?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, he thought Weyerhaeuser was doing all right. He came up here and he was put in charge of the shops up here at Camp 8. And T.P. Jones was put in as a general superintendent. But at that time, T.P. only got 300 hours a month. And everybody thought that was terrible money.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: A lot or a little?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: A lot. And it was for that day then. Laird was assistant superintendent at Potlatch. He got about $25 a day. Well, my boys are making more than that on the section now.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Laird got 25 a day?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah. And everybody thought that was terrible money. Well, it was at that time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you know Deary at all? Did you see him talk to him? What was he like? You said he couldn't read and write. And you said he was pretty tough… is that right?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah… he was a woman chaser.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's what I've heard.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah. He liked his women. Dolly Wood then. She was a pretty girl there at Palouse. His house. He rented a house in Palouse when he first come down at the lower end of Palouse. And they went around from the first floor up through the second at the front. And one morning, he'd get up about 5 o'clock, and he'd open and shut the front door and make it sound like he'd left. But he went back and got in bed with Dolly Wood then, the hired girl. One morning, Mrs. Deary was standing in the bay window upstairs, and she heard the door open and shut, but the building come off of the porch and across this yard going down to the mill. And she got suspicious right away. She slept downstairs and she went right into the bedroom. There old Bill was in bed with Dolly. She says, young lady, you get up and get your clothes and your suitcase and you get out of here. She says you're fired. Well.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I don't imagine that stopped Bill though.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No. He got a room up town in a lodging house, and he'd go out at the back way and come up into the alley that run down through where the rooms were. And the women would go up the front way and go into the room.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he leave home after his wife?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No. ... He just had another place to take the women. Well, Dolly played along with him for a year, and then she decided she wanted some money. And she commenced to pad herself. She says, Bill, you've got me in the family way and you've got to do something about it. All right, all right. I'll fix it up. But he neglected to do anything. She kept padming herself and getting a little bigger all the time. Finally she got her mother in on it, and she called old Bill at Puddle Hatcher's. She says, she's home. And Bill hadn't pulled away the phone booth. She said, Mr. Deary, you've got my daughter in trouble. You've got to do something about it. All right, all right. He says, I'll be right down. And he did. He come down. Well, Dolly says, I want three thousand dollars. We'll need that to raise and take care of that child. Old Bill gave her three thousand dollars. Then she took off her pads and went to the dances and she had a good time. But she saved that money. She didn't spend it recklessly. She still continued to work.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: I came to Bovill about that time. I didn't know much about him after that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it just Bill she fooled around with or was she really a... Oh, there was others. Yeah, she was a whore.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yes a private. She was an awful pretty girl.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was she pretty young when she was working at the Deary's?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yes, she was eighteen or nineteen. Just a young lady. She'd go to the dances and she was a wonderful dancer. She'd put a little bells on her shoes. She'd kick her feet around and bring them bells… she was classy.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But you don't know what became of her after you came to Bovill?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No… i don't know whether she ever got married or what became of her.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I heard there was an awful lot of... Oh, houses of ill repute and in Palouse in the really early days along with that.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: The houses of prostitution was on the side of the hill in the trees. You could see that big red light at night.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: They had a red light?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, they had a red light. You know, a sheriff from Colfax came up and talked to Tom Hopkins. He said, Tom, these houses got a reputation for being a house of prostitution. Tom says, I don't know, but as such well he did. It was illegal, you know, a house of prostitution. She was ugly. But, old Tom didn't know anything about them. They hear him tell it, but they know all about it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: The sheriff didn't do anything?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: The sheriff didn't do anything.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, did Bill Deary... I've heard about Bill Deary that he was about the toughest one in the bunch.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: He was really a strong man who wouldn't mind standing up and taking the guy down by punching him in the jaw. He was no longer a jack. He sure was that way. He never changed. He was just like one of them old time lumberjacks. Yes, he was that way. He'd fight if he had to, but of course nobody would fight him. He was a big shot, and they didn't want to get in bad with him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he go around looking for fights?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No, he wasn't coursing at all. His biggest trouble was women. He had quite a few of them lined up.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He and his wife managed to live with it, though.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Oh, yes, he was in his position at that time. She was quite famous as Bill Deary's wife. She'd go on the train to go to Spokane or anything, and of course they had a lot of women. Conductors and everybody looked up to her, and it was Mrs. Deary and this and that. They gave her a great deal of attention, and she liked that. She didn't want to lose her reputation with old Bill.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But it was common knowledge anyway that Bill was fooling around.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yes, everybody knew it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: She wasn't really fooling anybody. Was the brass in those early days like Deary and the people that lived on Nob Hill there in Potlatch, did they keep pretty separate from the ordinary lumberjacks?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yes, they were inclined to. There was a clerk up here at Camp 8. He started, and then he went to Deary. But them Bohunks from the Balkans came over and went to work, a big bunch of them into the camps. Their names were such that it was easy. Now the clerk, he forged quite a lot of checks to some one of these fellows by their name. He got away with it. They never caught him while he was up here, forging those checks. There was a clerk, a storekeeper at Deary that told me afterward, the trouble with him, he got married and he started out on the honeymoon. They ran out of money and he forged a check on an old lumberjack. Well, when the check came into the bank at Deary, Deary knew this fellow, was a personal friend of his, and he knew that that wasn't his check. They sent the sheriff after this clerk, and they picked him up on the train with his bride. I don't know what he got out of it, but he got a trip.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: He got away with it with those Bohunks forging their names, because they wasn't anybody that recognized it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you hear that story about that fight, that knife fight in Elk River where that Bohunk got killed?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How did you hear that happen?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: My brother over here was in the beer parlor when that happened. He saw there was Big Red. I followed by the name of Piwash. He'd done the stabbing, and he stabbed Big Red three, four times from the back. Finally, Big Red heeled over the bed, but he'd been stabbed four or five times before he fell. And Byers here was there. He said that the sheriff came over from Moscow, and they hid Piwash under the bed in the bunkhouse. The sheriff didn't look under the beds. He just went into the bunkhouse and looked through the bunks, all the bunks, and didn't see anybody. So he left. Then in three, four days they took Piwash out. Followed by the name of Mike Bubley. Mike is living here, I guess, in Spokane.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about him?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: He was with him when he'd done that stabbing. He held up over Piwash all his life. When Piwash died, Bubley got all his possessions. But in about two years, Piwash came back, and he went into the logging business. He worked here for years as a depot. Bubley worked as a general manager for him. When Piwash died, Bubley took over all his possessions.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was there any motive for the killing that Byers knew about?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No… he was drunk and shooting off his mouth. He was quarreling with five or six of them Bohunks. Old Sam was behind him, and he stabbed him. Well, in about two years after this Byers was downtown, and he saw a little bald-headed fella, and he recognized him. He said, That's the man that did that stabbing. I stood back and watched him, but he couldn't approve anything, and he didn't turn him in. Bubley stayed here and was a good, law-abiding citizen and logged for several years. Mike Bubley was his foreman, but that was big red, a red-headed lumberjack, a big fella. Bubley stabbed him four or five times. That's how many people were there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you first came to Bovill, when you first came here, that was right after they started the town?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, they hadn't started yet. I worked in the summer. They were building a railroad that was behind them. I worked down at Helmer. Helmer wasn't there, and it was a camp. I worked at the camp, and they saw timbers for the bridges. Dad and Felton had a little saw mill portable. They saw ties and timbers for bridges. They sawed them out, and teams would haul them out and deliver before they were going to use them. Well, Helmer had just been surveyed and hadn't started yet, but it was only at the point of starting, and Bovill wasn't started.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So you were sawing these bridges that they were making were for the railroad?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, they were… they had a 25-horse compound thrashing machine engine that ran the saw mill. I was running the engine. That was about eighteen.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was there a lot of activity going on around there at the time?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yes. Yes, it was getting ready to—the railroad was building, and there was a lot of them foreigners that was doing the work. They were building into Bovill. I came up to Bovill when there was this old hotel down here that Mrs. Bingham has, was the only building in here. That was a summer resort by Bovill. There was a bunch of young millionaire girls and boys that were coming out here every summer. He had about 20 saddle horses, and they'd give down those horses, and they'd ride over to Clarkia and over to Elk River. There was just trails those days. There wasn't roads.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where did they come from? From Moscow?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: They came from these. They were millionaire families, most of them. They were a wealthy class of people. They liked to get into the mountains in the summer and spend the summer in the mountains riding horseback. That was quite a sport. The girls all liked it, and the fellows liked to do what the girls did. They'd saddle up these horses and chase over the country.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you get to talk to those rich kids much?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No, I didn't… we came to Bovill in the fall, and they had left, gone back home. What were the Bovills like, the Mr. and Mrs.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Hugh and Charlotte Bovill?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: They were English. They came from England out here, and he opened up that resort. She was equipped to handle it in good shape. She understood handling the wealthy people. Bovill, he had the towns surveyed. Old Bill Deary wanted the town site to sell. Bovill wouldn't let him have it. He says, I'll tell you, Bovill, if you don't let me have the town site here, I won't put the mail here. I'll go to Elk River. He went up there, and he got the town site, and he put the mail in up there. He was thinking of putting that mail, and he was planning to put it in Bovill. Yes, and it went into Bovill, and Bovill would have let him have the town site.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Why didn't Bovill want him to?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, he figured there'd be more money for him to keep it and sell it himself. Well, it became quite a little berg. In those days, there was about three grocery stores. There was two or three hotels. There was probably six, seven hundred lumberjacks around here. And the beer parlors, they was good money. They made good money.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I heard that Bovill had mixed feelings about turning this area into a lumbering place because it was so pretty before it was touched.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, I suppose they did. They didn't like the idea, but they couldn't prevent that. Where out in what to Boise, and he dealt with the estate and got this timber at about a dollar a thousand. Think of it. And it wasn't long until they were paying $14 to $15 a thousand on the stump. But that was big money in those days.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was the Bovill Hotel the center of town in the first few years of Bovill? Was it the big meeting place?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, I don't know if they met that very much, but it was the only hotel that started. But there was two or three after that. There was one down on the corner where the fire station is now. That whole block burnt out. There was a problem that sold a dray. He'd give $1200 cash for the dray and give him the dray of the town. But he went to bed up there, and he had this money in his pocket. Well, everybody claimed that that fire was started by—he burnt up. He said that whoever started that fire went in and killed him and took the money, and then burnt the whole block out. It swept clear through that block. There was all wooden buildings. Then they went to work, and they rebuilt them in brick. Old A. Wilson built the hotel there where it's taken out now. He put that in, and Old A. made good. He had lots of business.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That fire, that was on the 4th of July?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, just about.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: About 1914?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, 1914.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What happened? Do you remember that night yourself? Were you around?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yes, I lived here in this house. I was married. We went downtown and watched that fire burn the whole block up. The bank was in this end, and the grooming house was on the far end. Well, the fire started in the lodging house, and it swept right through. Took the bank and whole. Old A. Wilson had a big hotel there then, but they all rebuilt. They built it in brick.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How did you fight it then? Were people trying to fight the fire? Was it just burning?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, they couldn't do anything. All they could do was stab them and watch it burn. They didn't have much water. Of course, they did have the tank up on the hill where it is now. It had a little water, but it was useless. The fire swept all over the block.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And this man was missing and found dead?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: He was burned up in the lodging house.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was he the only one there?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: He was the only one that lost his life, but he went to bed about midnight. The fire started right after that. Everybody figured in those days, he had $1,200 or $1,400 on him. They went in and killed him and took the money and set the building afire. It burned the whole block up. Then they rebuilt it in brick, as it now stands.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you remember in 1910 those terrible fires that they had in the country around here? What do you remember about that being like?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, I helped put fire on several of them. But the worst of them was when this fire came down the draw over here. It jumped across the meadow for a quarter of a mile. It lit on this side and it went by this house in a big roll of fire. A racehorse couldn't have got away from it. But there was 300 men from Potlatch that just got here on the train. They took all the women and kids out of Bovill on flat cars and took them down to Potlatch. They kept them down there two or three days and took care of them. Then they brought them home. But this fire, it burned this whole country for a couple of miles back. They're through here to where it went up onto the hill and the mountains back to us here. I don't know, check these 300 men and slow down to where they could get in front of it and stop it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was this the, this was the Beals Butte fire, the one they call the Beals Butte fire?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: It sort of started up towards Beals Butte?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yes, it started there to put a Beals Butte and come down the draw. It had been burning for a week. But one hot afternoon, it was a little earlier than this in July, and it was hot. Well, that fire, one afternoon it commenced to travel. And the farther it come, the faster it cut. And it jumped. Those meadows took on to this side. They went through here in a big roll of wire. By my place, it missed this place by a couple hundred feet.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What did you do when it came?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, my wife had gone with her people down to Potlatch on the train, but I stayed back. We'd take water up onto the building. If any sparks or anything fell, and start a fire, we'd put it out. And I saved the house.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did sparks hit the roof?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yes. There was some sparks as it hit the roof. Dad stayed over there to his house. And I was here. We would pack water up on the top, and if a fire little pot-fired start, I'd throw water onto it. Saved the houses.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How hot was it?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Oh, it wasn't too hot over on the side here because it caused the wind to come in and hit it on the side.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you hear about the story about how the train came into Bovill, how the bridge was burning and the train came in anyway? What's the story about that?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, the bridge underneath was a fire a little bit, but it wasn't hers, any. Shea engine had come down from Cougar Meadows. That's where that is back in here. It came down. Now, Camp 8 up here was in under the hill, and the fire went over the top and didn't get the shot and the cold hawk. So, that bridge crossing the crypt up here, it got a fire a little bit and was burning when the train went over it, but it wasn't hurt any yet. And they put it out and saved the bridge.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What caused the fire to stop instead of taking the whole town with it?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, the fire didn't come through on a line about 200 feet out here. And it went on and it missed Bovill. It didn't spread sideways. Because there was a lot of men from out of that were brought in on flat cars, about 300. They lined out and stopped all chances of the fire getting to the town or doing any more damage than they could help. But when that fire went by out here, you couldn't have worked in front of it. Because it rolled by in a big roll of fire, just rolling. And the boys were going traveling too. But it went on about a mile. But after that, it slowed it down to where they could get in front of it and stop it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When you say a roll of fire, was it like just one sheet rolling?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yes… just a big roll of fire went through. The heat was running everything below it. That was the most terrible, the poorest fire I ever saw. But that sure traveled from over any under to up above here. It would have got anything in front of it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I had heard from someone that said that people were praying to stop the fire.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Oh yes, there was a lot of praying. And they contributed it. Their prayers had a lot to do with it and saving the town. I had just been married. I was married in May, no in April. And the fire was in July. The leg on that piece of furniture that it broke, where they took it out. They took all my furniture out downtown and took it out in the meadow and dumped it in the meadow so that the fire wouldn't get it. But the house didn't burn up.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: The leg broke when they were moving it?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: But when they took it out of the off of the wagon, why they let it down onto one leg and it broke it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where did you meet your wife?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: She lived down here in town. I met her and she was a pretty woman and a pretty girl… his wife was...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: She is pretty.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, I was practically 30 years old and she was only 18. I thought if I was going to get married, I'd better get married.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: In those days, do you remember what courting was like?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Oh yes… she was just... Dippy about me. And I was out of bad luck.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What would you do for dates in those days? To go out to be together and that sort of thing?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: There were lots of parties in town. People would get together nights and parties.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: At that time, was there still drinking going on?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Oh yes, there was lots of drinking. They were moonshining. You see, they didn't allow no liquor to be sold here in Bovill from the start. The Potlatch controlled it and they didn't want liquor houses. They had the authority that they could not allow it. Well, there was lots of moonshining. Pearls that lived here. Made living by bootlegging.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about... I know other places at the dances they used to have moonshine and sometimes they get pretty rowdy.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yes, generally do.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about the girls? Wouldn't that be pretty rough to have that going on around them?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: They didn't seem to mind it. Of course, there were two or three different classes. The girls that went to the dances, why they... They were more of that type and they didn't mind overdrinking a little bit. My brother Frank, he was... He danced and drank. And he was one of the musicians that played for the dance. Myers over here was pretty wild at that time too, but he was just a young fellow about 18.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, what did you do when you were a wild kid in those days? Didn't you have motorcycles to go screaming around on the way they do now so much?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, I had a motorcycle that I taught him, 12. And I'd take the girls riding cars and they called it the Sparking Machine. But it was a twin cylinder. It was a good motorcycle. It'd be about what they'd pay about $600 for now, but it only cost me $175 in those days. I went up to Spokane to buy an Indian motorcycle. But I went down to the Indian and he took me in. He had about half a dozen secondhand ones, but he didn't have no new ones. Well, I told him, I said, I didn't come up here to buy a new... Or a secondhand motorcycle, I want a new one. Well, he says, we've got new ones down here in the warehouse. Well, I said, that's what I want. I went up to town and there was another motorcycle outfit. They were just taking a new one out of the crate. I went in, I was standing looking at it. And the fella said, you better let me sell you a new motorcycle. Well, I said, that's what I come up here to buy, was a motorcycle. Well, he got busy right now. He said, you stick around here till I get this set up and I'm going to take you ride. And he took me out and boy, there was a hill that sure went up. And he put me on in front of him and he went up that hill like it wasn't there. I thought that was just what I wanted. And I bought it.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: I paid him cash for it. And I was in the habit of putting them out on payments. But he was glad to get the money out of it. Or he could turn right around and get more. The Indian man who run across me with this new motorcycle, he said, I thought you were going to buy one of me. Well, I said, I went to you first. And you showed me a lot of secondhand stuff and I didn't want it. And I went up here and found this man taking the new one out of a crate and I bought it. And he didn't like it very well. He didn't say no more.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, when the young guys were drinking and driving around in Bovill in those days, what about the law? Do you have any trouble with Pat from Pat Malone?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No, they got along with old Pat pretty well. Old Pat was a peculiar old fella. A sheriff came up from Moscow and got him. They understood it beguile. One of the foremen had some moonshine in his car. He got Pat and they went up to Collins up here and the car was standing there. And the sheriff sent old Pat over to search the car, see if there was any moonshine. Old Pat went over and he saw some moonshine in his car. He reported to the sheriff because he didn't find any. He didn't want to get a big deal. He wasn't selling it. He would buy it to drink. Old Pat knew it and he didn't want to get him. Big Gill was a Frenchman, a big man. He'd take a peavey and he could break the handle out of it right now. He was a powerful man. I've heard he was really a quiet man too. He didn't say much. He didn't have any discernment to speak of.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: But he was a good logger. And he had a camp of a couple hundred men.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about Pat… i've heard that Pat used to really like his moonshine himself.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, he was quite a man to want to drink. He arrested the young fella down to Deary. They brought him up on the train and got down here to the depot. The lad jumped off the other side of the train when Pat wasn't looking. He took to his heels and old Pat shot up in the air to try to scare him to stop. The kids stubbed his toe and fell. Well, Pat said, I didn't want to shoot him, I didn't want to shoot him. But he just had to, had to. He thought he'd hit him. But he didn't. The kid jumped up and kept on going. He didn't get him. There were two whorehouses down here. They had about 12, 15 girls. There was a tough hombre that went down there one night. He had a six-year-old and he made these girls stand around, go out and get a bottle of beer and bring it in and open it up and give everybody a drink. He was having a lot of fun. One of them got away and went up and got old Pat. Pat went down and he opened the door and stepped in and put a gun right on to this fella. He said, get your hands up and do it quick. Well, the fella did. He arrested him. I guess he got a jolt out of it. You mean he got a... He got sent to Boise.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, that's about the only case I ever knew about. He really was in the bite of the line and he had to do something and he really done it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He was in the what? In the bite of the line?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: That's an old expression of fury and bad, to be in the bite of the line.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He had to do something. He didn't have any choice. Well, I've heard he just looked the other way an awful lot.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yes, he did. The young fella's here, he didn't want to get them into trouble. The others over here were pretty rowdy in those days and he was drinking moonshine. He was husky. An awful stout man, very young fella. But I didn't drink or carouse because I was religious. I went to church and that's where I met my wife, was a church. I went to church and that's where I met my wife.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You catered to the lumberjacks and the camps?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yes. I came up to take pictures and I had a room at the hotel. They kept sending me, sending up for me to come down and take some pictures of them. I told the fellas, I said, I'm going to go down there and take pictures and take it and trade. Finally, they sent word up that they had money. They'd pay for their work as well as anybody else. They didn't expect me to trade it out. So we needed some money pretty bad. I said to my partner, I said, let's go down and take good pictures. We can make fifty dollars in a couple of days. So we went down and we took pictures. I took the negatives down home. I had them in the cellar with my other negatives and my two sisters and mother. The girls found those negatives and they knew that those girls were prostitutes. They showed them to mother and they put me on the carpet. I told mother that I was just saying, we needed the money and we went down and took those pictures to get some quick money.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, she's kind of half believed me. I told her we didn't take anything out and trade.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was the lumberjacks buying these pictures?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No… the girls wanted pictures of themselves. Lots of them had silk gowns that they paid two hundred and fifty dollars for. They made easy money and they spent it. When I took the pictures up in the next morning, they called me at the hotel and wanted to know how the pictures were. I said, I'm going to come down in a little while with proofs to show you. Well, she says, this is no place for a preacher's son.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were you a preacher's son?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah… but it was because of the fact that I wouldn't have anything to do with him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were you already married by then? This is when you were still a young, eligible bachelor.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: I was a young fellow then. Probably four years before I got married.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, Pat put up with those places, right?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: He didn't object to them being married.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he collect money from them for staying in operation?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: I suppose he did. I expect they paid a fine. Most places like that did. Troy had a house or two. The sheriff in Moscow would generally collect money.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What were you doing in those days for a living? Were you taking photographs? Was that how you were making a living?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No. I was working up to the shop in the cable. And on Saturdays and Sundays and nights after work, why I take pictures? I made my own videos. I was more in the pictures than I did working.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Where did you get into the picture-taking business from?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, when I was in Palouse. I wanted to learn the picture business. A new man had bought it named Jocelyn and bought the picture.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Were you then?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Oh, I was probably 19.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: And you went in to ask him if you could work with him?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yes… he took me in. I watched him do the work. He bought the gallery of a fellow that had been there. The fellow wasn't doing very well. He sold it to Jocelyn. And he thought that Jocelyn wouldn't make it, and he'd get the place back. That's what he thought for Jocelyn. He got a man to come in, and he sent him out to solicit work, giving him $5 worth, or $2.00 and a half. They would have to buy a... make a payment down and buy a certificate. That's when they presented at the gallery why they'd get this picture taken. And he got $500 or $600 worth of work there. No time. He had a salesman that went into the field soliciting the work. Well, when people got it, a dollar, a dollar and a half tied up, why they would try to get the benefit of it. He didn't land off of business there for six weeks.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: He paid the gallery off, and both the fellow that he bought off and the bank then, often told me, he says the bank didn't act as though they were pleased at me making the payment. But he says, that don't make no difference to me. He says, they thought that they'd go back and maybe have their money without them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Oh, you mean the bank would get the business back again?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, they thought that this photographer would get his place back and have the money that he sold it for too, but he didn't.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, he took you in, and did you work for him for free or did you get paid or what?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No, I didn't get paid. I just helped him in all his work, and I learned the business. Well, I went to Grangeville from here. I went to, I met a fellow come in here and set up a little gallery downtown. He took pictures before Christmas, and he'd done the land off of business. He got me to come down and help him. He couldn't work for AZO. Well, I said, I've used AZO for years, and I don't have no trouble with it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Work with what?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: AZO Postcard… that's the name of the postcard. He couldn't work it. We took a lot of postcards, set up and got ready to make the postcards. He said, you mix up the developer. So I went in and I weighed all the chemicals and mixed it according to oil. He'd come in and he said, what are you doing? I said, mix him up the developer. Well, he says, I never took all that pains. Well, I said, that's why you've had trouble. I said, you've got to get these chemicals according to oil. We run out, 500 or 600 postcards. He'd come in and put them on a big sheet if we had stretched out to dry. He'd turn them over and look at them. He says, I can't see why that they don't spot up like they did with me. Well, I said, it's because you didn't mix your chemicals right. I said, these cards are made to give service where the developer is mixed according to directions. We put out a lot of postcards and had no trouble. Then he wanted me to go with him. We went over to Grangeville and put him in a gallery.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: But we didn't do very good. Didn't make it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So you came back?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: So I quit the business. You see, he was a gambler, a tinhorn, and boy, he was good. The night we left here, he went into a game and they took $300 away from him. We went down to Lewiston and he sat in the game and they took $300 more.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You know if he was honest?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Oh, no. He had a way of gyppoing him. I don't know how it was, but he was a tinhorn. He was good at it. Then we went up to Grangeville and he sat in the game there and he took another $300. Well, he went down to White Bird and he stayed there for a couple of months. He came back and I said, Linux, I said, don't get around this bunch here. Well, they're pretty mad that you took them for $300 and they're laying for you and they'll take you. He said, that bunch can't take me. Well, they got him drunk and that night they took $600 away from me and broke him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Gambling with him?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah… and boy, he was just sick the next day. He was broke. They took all his money, got him drunk. Well, I said, I told you to stay away from them. They played together and they took you. They figured don't get me in the damn it. Well, he says if I hadn't got drunk, they wouldn't have got me. But he got drunk and they took him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it hard for you to learn the trade over in Palouse? Was there much to photography?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Oh, there was quite a little bit, but I was anxious to learn and I paid attention to everything I learned fast. And I got good.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you stay with him for very long?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No, a couple of months. And then I came up here and went to work and I got myself a little camera and I took postcards on the lumberjacks.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Why did you take pictures of mostly?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: They were just mostly lumberjacks.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What were those guys like, the old time lumberjacks that were in the camps around here?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, they were pretty rare fellows.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Pretty what?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Pretty good fellows as a rule. Now, Doc Dart's son, he would school us out. His father wanted him to get a job and earn a little money for the summer. Well, his mother says, now, son, when you get up to Mobile and Mon-Man Lumberjacks, they're going to be rough men. And when you go into the table, they were more like a bunch of hogs than like people. And he told me, he says, I thought I was coming into an awful bunch of men. But he'd been over to college and he learned a lot of smart, I like to talk to them students at the table. He said, why don't you go over? And he wanted the gravy and he says, Joe, he says, pass the smear, will you? Joe looked at him and he says, you have to talk English to me if you want me to pass you anything. He says, I don't understand that kind at all. When he went back, he said, Mother, you've got the wrong opinion of that lumberjacks. He says, they're nice. At the table, they say, please pass the gravy, please pass the potatoes, and please pass the bread. He says, they're a lot smaller than the college students over to Pullman.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, his mother couldn't hardly believe it, but he told her they were. He says, they're real gentlemen at the table. And they ask for, please pass this and please pass that. Ma 'am got a nickname for it. They call it what it is. He says, you've got the wrong opinion about that lumberjacks, but they're not the kind of men you think they are. The steel gang was serbians, mostly serbians, that come over from the old country. Mrs. Jones, Mrs. T. P. Jones would go in and sit down at the table at noon and eat with them for us. They'd not know it. Mrs. McPhee and her husband were the foremen of the steel gang. She wouldn't let him or you couldn't get hurt at the table with them, not with them foreigners at all. She said, they're just like a bunch of pigs. And she says, I don't want to eat with them.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: But Mrs. Jones would go in and sit down and... They fed off for good those days. They had everything on the table you could think of. And those fellas come over from Serbia that never had anything much to eat at home… why… it was a wonderful thing to them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I've heard different things about the fighting that went on among the lumberjacks. I've heard it said that they didn't used to fight in the camps hardly, but they would in town.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah they'd get drunk and fight. They didn't allow no fighting in camp. Foremen would treat her that. The depot agent, the person they had down here, he quit the depot and he went to clerking for McFarland, the steel gang. And in those days, the beef only got Potlatch. 8 cents a pound. They'd buy a whole beef at 8 cents a pound. It was hung in a meat house on a flat cover. So the air would get to it, but the sun couldn't. And McFarland would go in and he'd cut the porterhouse out of the stake and take it for himself. And this clerk went to work for him. He noticed that. So he said to T.P. Jones, one day that's the general superintendent. He says that McFarland cuts the porterhouse out of the beef and takes it for him and his wife. He says, is there any objection if I take another for that for me and my wife?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Jones says no. He says, help yourself. Jones, of course, accompanied about 8 cents a pound. He didn't think nothing of that price. So he went to taking the porterhouse. He had the advantage of McFarland because the meat would come in and be put in the meat house. And he was right by the office. Of course, he was the clerk. He'd go out and he'd get the beef before McFarland could. McFarland got pretty mad about it. Him and this clerk, they got into a fight. They went in down onto the ground. Mrs. McFarland kind of wrapped her in it and they sparred around. Neither one could hit the other. And finally she got disgusted with him. She says, you fellas got this fighting out. She said, I could lick either one of you myself. She says, we won't have any more fighting. Just cut it out. They did.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, I've heard if the two Jacks were, lumberjacks were in a fight and one of them got knocked down, the other guy would stomp him with his cork boots.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, sometimes there was one fool around here that got into a fight down at Princeton, knocked the foreigner down, went on to him with his boots, killed him. Kicked his head with those cork boots, killed him. But he had stabbed this fellow a couple of times. And of course when he come to court, he showed these wounds where this fella had stabbed him. Of course the court dismissed the case and said that he was justified in protecting himself. Even if he did kill the other fellow, the other fellow was stabbing him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: These foreigners that worked on the section and the steel gang, were they, they get less money than the other lumberjacks did? Were they?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, I don't know what they did. I think they thought about the same thing. But, you see, they worked at the steel gang and they, they were foreign. And McFarland, he took about five dollars a month off of each one of them. Well, it was forty of them, well it counted quite a bit. It was more than his salary, maybe more than double his salary. And the same way in the woods, those foremen took the advantage of those foremen and they paid three to five dollars a month off of them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, how did he have the right to do that?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: They didn't have no right. They just do it, the clerk. They'd have the clerk take the money out of it, charge it to them on the warning and then write them a check for it. There's always somebody that's taking the advantage of the other fellow if they can.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, these foreigners, they were easier prey because they didn't know the ways that this country is so good, huh?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, they didn't know. They were willing to work for anything they could get.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did they mix much with the other, with the other people, with the other lumberjacks or did they have to keep to themselves?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: They had to keep to themselves, but well, oh, they made some friends. A lot of them went back when the Balkan War broke out with Turkey. But every one of them was killed that went back. There was one young fellow that worked in the shop. He said, you know, I'm not going back. He said, I was in one war back there. My brother was killed right beside me. And he says a whole lot of the boys went down when the Turks fired and killed him. And he says, I'm not going back. He says, I can make a living. He says, my father was what you call wealthy back there. But he says, I won't give it if I don't go back. But I'm what good is it to you if you go back and get killed? And he was right. Every one of them boys that went back, they, there's none of them ever come back again. They all died.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: This Balkan war was between the Turks and who?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, the Turks and Bulgaria and Serbia. Those little Balkan countries.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, do you think that they didn't mix out of choice or you think they couldn't have even if they wanted to because they were foreigners?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: They were foreigners and they couldn't talk English much and they didn't try to mingle with the old time number tracks. Some of them did. Some of them was pretty smart and to talk good English. One fellow, they called him old Job. He put monkey around and he didn't do too much work. But old build area was up there and he saw that he wasn't working very much and he walked up and fired him. He said, me, me work. You, you know, like you quit. Told. Old build area. Well, after build left by Dave Brown, this fellow was working for Dave Brown. Dave let him go right ahead and work. Because old build was on… yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was buyers certain that he saw Sam Piwash that he was the guy? Was he sure?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, he was sure.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Because I know that Mike Bubley, I met him in Spokane and he is told he has said that that's one thing in in trees grew tall that he thinks isn't true. He says Mike Bubley says that Sam Piwash wasn't even there. That's what he says.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Bubley would protect him because he got all of his calling to him. Bubley was, Piwash was pretty well healed when he died and Bubley got everything… yeah… he had him in the old folks homes over there at Marsh Yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's when he knew that it was Piwash.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He didn't know the man when he didn't know the man.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Bohunk was all that he knew that. That's what was stated a bull. That's what he was saying. He was a Bohunk. A big red… killed him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was big red a Bohunk too?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No, he was a lumberjack. But he was drunk. And he was throwing his voice and bulling these Bohunks out. He didn't like them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Do you think these guys ran into much what you call discrimination like that? These Bohunks because they were foreigners?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Oh, not too much. Not too much either. Simply because they didn't try to mingle. Some of them were pretty smart. They had good jobs. They talked good English. Well, all of them, Pudnier, went back to the Balkan War and they never returned.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I've heard that most of these old lumberjacks were bachelors. Yeah.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: They wouldn't have any of them to speak of that were married men. They've been bachelors all their life. Most of them come from Wisconsin or Minnesota back there in the woods department. They came out here and went to work and they were following up their trade.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would you say they were more solitary men or more sociable?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, the old lumberjacks were quite sociable. But they were pretty rough, some of them. They were working. There was one big lumberjack. He was pretty rough in his talk. And there was a fellow had his boy working with him and he was religious and was a church member. He went to this big lumberjack. He says, I don't want you swearing and cursing and using the language you do in front of my boy. Well, the old lumberjack had made him mad. He says, you just forget. He says, I'm not taking orders from you. I talk the way I want to. And it made him all the worse. He'd get around where the boy was and he'd use violent language. And lots worse than he did. Because it made him mad. Because this fellow didn't want him swearing in front of that boy. He said, you needn't bring your churchology in here and go to try and preach to me. He said, I don't fall for it. And he was a wicked old rascal.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did he have a nickname, this guy?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No. Not till I know of. I don't even remember his name now. Old Frank Hatfield come from Virginia coal mines. He was in the Hatfields where one of the feuds back there. He pulled out and left and come west. He told me, he says, I got out of there because you'd be killed when you weren't expecting it. He said, I just pulled out while I had my life. He said, they never got a chance to get me.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was he working out here in the woods?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, he was night watch down here at the shop for a long time after he got old. Night watch jobs was kind of a job for that kind of men. It was really tiring. Couldn't do much work. But they could night watch him do that kind of work.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you ever hear of any feuds or know of any feuds around here?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That seems like something that mostly went on back in the east. Maybe because, I wonder why, maybe because the families had been living there for so long they got to hate each other for a long period of time.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, it was kind of the way the country's too. Old Mike Welch told me. He said when I was a young fella back there, one night there was a German. He'd come from the old country and they rounded him up and took him out and hung him. But he says when we had him, we was on the run and making him run. And he dropped his worship pipe and broke it. And he was pretty mad. Now he says, see you at your dump. You made me break my worship pipe. Well, they told him that they were going to make him break more than that before he was through with it. And they took him out into the woods, put a rope around his neck and throwed it up over the limb. And now they said, if you've got anything to say, say it before we put you up. Well, he says, I see you fellas mean business. He says, before I left Germany, I killed my wife. And he told about his Scott ugly work in the past years.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Confessed to them and they stretched him up and hung him, left him hanging. Tied the rope up and left him hanging there for a lot of fun. But he said there was lots of that kind of work among them vigilantes.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was that World War I, you think?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No, that was before that. That was long about six.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What were they going after this guy for? Did they have any reason to suspect him?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: He was in bad in the community and they were going to lynch him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, they used to have vigilantes in the farming in the country out here, I know that. Didn't you ever hear about them over in Colfax and Palouse?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No, there was one lynching in Colfax. When I was a young fella, they went into the jail, they went and got the sheriff, took him down and made him unlock the jail and let him in. And they took this fellow out.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Yeah, is it?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: They hung him… his name was..… oh, I know. Ed Hill. Ed Hill, that's it. I know the story, I've heard it… yeah… i heard it. I heard it… that was mostly...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Was it Odd Fellows?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No, it wasn't. No, it wasn't. It was... They... Oh, it's kind of a religious lodge.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Oh, Masons?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, the Masons.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Most of those guys that were in the lynch mob.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, they were Masons, of course. This... This fellow had... killed a mason in so much... The other Masons got together and they went and got him. And hung him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, I've heard there was two guys hung at the same time there, that hanging Colfax. There was another guy hung with Ed Hill, I don't remember his name.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: I didn't know of that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's what I thought, anyway.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: They might have been.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you hear about when Agnus Leener got killed? Agnus Leener here?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yes. Yes. You see, he was over in the mine, and the tunnel went back in there three, four hundred feet. And he had the Leener girl back in there. And he... She had turned him down and wouldn't marry him. And when he says, if you don't, ain't gonna marry me, I'll kill myself. And he had begun, oh, she said, don't do that. She said, shoot me. And he did. He shot her. And Billy Omar, and Dad, they started to go in after him, and he shot down the tunnel, and the ball ricocheted around through the tunnel. And they jumped back out, and they stood by the side of the tunnel until he came out, and they grabbed him. They brought him over, and... he was sent to Boise, to the van.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He didn't die. He didn't get killed. He didn't get killed.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: He killed this girl… leener girl.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Tell him what he told me, that they thought he raped her before he killed her.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, he might have. Nobody knows what he'd done. But the story that he told was, as I told you, that it might have been different than the real facts.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you ever see Pack Sack Dick, Dick Farrell?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yes, I know Dick well. I always liked Dick. He was a lumberjack preacher. Boy, he could really lay it down to him. But of course, the Presbyterian Church paid him as a... preacher for the lumberjacks. Yeah, but that's... paying him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You didn't Potlatch ...?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: He did missionary work in the camps. I don't know. I know that's what it was Potlatch paying him to do. I've been in camp when he preached.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What were his sermons like?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Oh, they were good. He'd tell them. He didn't putty-foot it tall. He'd tell them that they couldn't drink and carouse and carry on.

speaker: Unknown Speakers
words: He's downtown. Come here. You said you'd only been there six months. Well, that's what it was around town. That's a bunch of who it was. Well, that's what started around town here. Yeah, that's what I thought. That's what I thought. That's what somebody was talking about on town. The world told me that. I come into town here one day and... somebody said that the doctor told him he only had six months to live. That's why I come down today to see what was wrong with him. Oh, he's getting better all the time...

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, I just got one more question about Dick Farrell. Now stop. That is, was he into... did he give him a lot of hellfire and brimstone, or was he... pretty understanding of their... those guys? You've heard Dick preach, didn't you? Kim? Dick Farrell? Dick Farrell?

speaker: John Sanderson and Unknown Speakers
words: No, he wasn't there. I wasn't here then. Sure, no. Maybe I'm probably out. I wouldn't preach. Yeah, I... I've been in camp. I'm scalin' when he'd come in and hold meetings. He didn't push his little... He told him what they were... Oh, he told him I have, boys. Where they were going. I stopped seeing Emma the other day. We were up there. Yeah. We was up there. Pleasure. I sent that. I've got to go back Monday. Yeah. Well, I've got to head back to the ranch. Yeah. No, I just stopped to see how Richard was. I've been worried about her, you know, that... Well, that's... I heard that. That's what the doctor told him. He says you haven't got anything to worry about. No. You just take this medicine, then. Yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He was a good man for the lumberjack. Well, he...

speaker: John Sanderson
words: He knew how to preach to them. Yeah. And he didn't pussy-foot talk. He told them right where they stood and what they could expect. He was right. They'd stand and listen to him. Wow.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: They seemed to like him a lot, too, from what I heard.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, they all liked it. Of course, he was honest in these preaching.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What would he tell them? How would you talk to a bunch of guys that were... that were not living the usual, you know, settled-down life with wives and families? Wouldn't it be harder to preach to a bunch of people like that?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: It was hard, and Dick was just the man that could. As I said, he didn't pussy-foot. And... he was right out in the open, what he was. Well, that's what they let the day-long do. He... He'd preach to them.

speaker: John Sanderson and Unknown Speakers
words: That's right. They thought the hill was gonna be... They'd do what they'd do down there. They ain't gonna do it. I can do my duty. He knows the way I do it. That's just too bad. You like to teach them, man. You just get to teach them. You got to be the right teacher. You got to teach them. Kids go right away. I heard me and all that. I mean... The other girls wasn't no question or nothing. They didn't want to... They wanted to go to the rest of these old dancers. Whack a jean all the time. We don't know all that. If you're gonna teach us science school, you got to get that out of your mind. You can't have that going, teaching you and that. They got mad, and they... So they kicked him out the door. We didn't kick him out. So the folks laughed, you know. Well, the little veteran told these girls to walk her to the kick yard there. Walking in one of... He's gonna turn him away in that, talk to him. You know, the old... The little veteran spangled out, so they got to kick the girls out. And he got mad in the way of the wet. The old thing made it to the kind of middle of the hood. Well, I didn't say that. I didn't... No, it was all packaged. They told us, well, you shouldn't tell them that. I'm gonna tell them. They told them what they're gonna do, what they're gonna do and everything. And then they found out, and out they went. So the folks were there, that walkers kind of... They kicked him out of the torch. Well, they didn't... They told them, I didn't kick them out. I wouldn't ever do it. I was gonna tell them in a nice way what I have to do. And I'm the one that... And I... One of them is, and I'm the one... The superintendent is the one that's the one and me. And I got good at what he says. Got one of those people who were saying, doing what I say. I can't do that. He's gonna wear a piece of cloth with it, push it. We're not gonna go on the bush and not push it. And we said, we said, but the water, if you've ever got mad, you can tell them nothing. So the president's got it all back over. That's made trouble.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You know, I think of a guy like Dick Farrow coming into camp and preaching to the lumberjack, and if he says to him, well, you're either gonna mend your ways or you're not gonna make it. Well... Then that might be pretty tough for a lot of guys to swallow, because the way they live in those days...

speaker: John Sanderson and Unknown Speakers
words: He'd come right out in the open and told them what they could expect, living the way they did. That way they'd walk it right down. It isn't hard to become a Christian and to live right. He says, you can just as well come out here drinking and swearing and cursing and... Walk it down the road. Live like these people. These people were lessons in the water. I didn't mean that. I didn't mean to keep them goes out. The other girl went and tore them off. I didn't mean to get mad. I was gonna tell them the nice way. But the people didn't... How many more did they throw at you anymore? Well, what was it like? I didn't get them out. You got that wrong. They did. They misunderstood. Well, that's what the son of a girl went and tore her eyes. And there was one that went and wasn't big. I said, you got to be big. I didn't even have to get them to go to the other side. Just got to talk to them and they had them to talk with. Told them the right way and I wasn't mad. I was gonna tell them, don't get them mad. Just tell them what I got to do. But they didn't want... If one got mad, the folks got mad and wasn't listening.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did you ever hear the story about Dick Farrell? There was once one or two guys that was giving him a hard time. They were getting in the way of him trying to preach a sermon. Yes. And he'd licked them. He licked them mad. He was a firefighter before he came out preaching.

speaker: John Sanderson and Unknown Speakers
words: He went back to college and they saw that he'd make a good preacher for the Lumberjacks. And that's what they got him into. But that was one fellow that had come to lick him. Dick licked him about a minute. He'd been a firefighter and he knew his stuff. Yeah, I don't know about that. I don't know about that. You know, you got to work. I guess he's a fucking little bit of a baby. Now you have to have him himself.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That's the story. Did I hear... I heard somebody say, well, you know a lot of them.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Right down there it's Bruce. There was a bunch of young fellas about 18 that was going to school. Every teacher that they'd get and bring in there, he'd lick them. The kids would lick them. And they sent them to another fellow that was a... He'd been a firefighter. And they got him to handle the school. The boys picked on him one day and he licked a whole bunch of them. He'd knock them down as fast as they'd get to him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Who was that?

speaker: John Sanderson and Unknown Speakers
words: That wasn't Tom. No. That's another one.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: That took care of the problem then.

speaker: John Sanderson and Unknown Speakers
words: That's Tom. He graduated over there to Moscow. They gave him a school out beyond Potlatch up on the... Creek. Oh. And there was a bunch up there that had run every teacher out. And Tom heard about it after he got to the school. But he said he was going to see it through. And one day at noon, this fella got up on the back of his seat and was sitting on it and winking at the others. Tom knew there was trouble going on. So he cleaned out a bunch of the seats. He made an opening in there. And he kept his back to this lad all the time while he was cleaning it out. He said, if the kid had been smart, he'd know what he was doing. But he said after he got it all cleaned out in good shape, he whirled and he grabbed that fella and he showed him right into the floor. And then he kicked him out, kicked him clean out of his house.

speaker: John Sanderson and Unknown Speakers
words: And then he went back. He says, now if there's any more of you fellas that want something, come on. He says, we can finish it all up in good shape now. But then he didn't come. And this lad went home and told his dad. His dad came down and he said to Tom, he says,… nesbitt, don't you think you're a little bit rough with the kid? Well, he says, I'll tell you, the kid, those kids intended to lick me. And he says, I just beat him with a punch. And he says, I know that this lad of yours was the ringleader. And he says, I grabbed him and I kicked him out. He can't come back to school, that's your guarantee, his conduct. Well, now he says, you take him home and talk to him and tell him that you're not sending him to school to fight, not to learn to fight. You're sending him there to learn to get an education. And Tom said that boy was a study good. Never caused any more trouble. One day he was over at the Pullman and he says, there's a big fella in there.

speaker: John Sanderson and Unknown Speakers
words: A ball uniform came up and he came up to Tom and he says, come over here, I want to introduce you to the man that made a man out of me. He introduced himself. He asked Tom, I remember you, but he says, you've got to be a big man.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: He says, Tom, do you think you could handle me like you did now? Well, Tom says, I could try. He says, I believe you tried. He said he was a fine lad and was going to college. But that made a man out of him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What happened in the schools when most of them had women teachers? How did they handle this rowdiness?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, they don't try to handle it anymore. ... In the old days, they always got the professor. Now, I was going to school in Palouse. Tommy Nichols, that's Mrs. Evans' father. He was 18 and a little shortfall and stubby and stout as a bow. I heard him say in the basement one day, as we said, Foster wasn't going to lick him. He said, I'll see to that. Foster was an awful man to lick. He went over and he grabbed, reached down to grab Tommy and shake him. And Tommy shot his fist up into Foster's nose. And then he, Foster rolled around over his shoulders. Tom couldn't get him down or he couldn't get the best of Tom. When the girls got out and went down and got for Professor Mokorski, he came up and came in and he said, Tom, he says, what's going on here? He says, I'm trying to get my books and go home and Foster won't let me. But the white stopped. Tom took his books and went home. I asked him down here one time.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: I said, Tom, do you remember that white? He says, you better do. He says, that's all the education I ever got. And he says, if I run across Foster today, I'd lick him. I said, he says, I don't care how old he is. I knock the tar out of him. He says, he ruined my education.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He couldn't go back to school after that, huh?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No, he didn't try to.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Did Foster have it in for him or did he do something real bad?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: No, that's the way he was if you weren't paying attention. When he was reading the story, if you were looking down and wasn't paying attention, he'd go down and grab you to shake you. That's what he took with Tom, which Tom didn't shake. But you say like these women teachers, they wouldn't try to do it themselves. They'd go and get a man to take care of the rowdy kids. They'd send them to the professor. Although there was one teacher that had my brother Frank when he was a kid downtown. They didn't have room in the big schoolhouse and she had to school downtown. Frank was going there. And she couldn't make him ball. She had a rowdy and she was licking him over the back. The professor come in and she stopped him. He says, Frank, he says, if I do right, I didn't give you a licking myself. But he says, I won't. Frank went back to his seat. When he'd come home away, his shirt was all stuck to him where she'd cut his back. Well, that's all right. Mother says to Frank, she says, she took his shirt off and washed the cuts. She says, you go up and show your back to Professor McCloskey and tell him what he said. I asked him if he didn't think he wasn't up. And Professor McCloskey looked at his back and he asked, he says, Frank, you've got too much. They shouldn't have licked you like that. And he went down and he told that woman never to lick another kid. He says, if he has spoke as a prosecutor, you do not stay up. Because his back is all cut up and you should be ashamed of yourself to lick a kid like that. And she never did lick anybody after that.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Oh, I want to ask you, what's the story on the IWWs? What did they do around here?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: They didn't do anything. But they had a reputation of wanting to do something. They had gunmen and watchmen out at the camps for IWWs. They had a house down here, but ten or fifteen of them would meet there and they'd have a speech as to what they wanted to do in the camps.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: But... But you said they didn't do anything. They didn't do any of the sabotage that some people say they do. They didn't sabotage anything.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: They're doing the thing.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I've heard old lumberjacks say that they were the ones that got the better conditions in the camps. Do you think the IWW did that?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, they improved the camps.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: How did they manage that?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, they... I'll tell you, at that time, the bedbugs was awful bad. And they didn't have anything to combat them. They'd run sulfur in the camp. Bedbugs were running on the outside. There were low buildings. They'd run on the outside and when the fumes were gone, they'd come back in. And when they got the spray that would kill them, why, they got rid of them. But before that, they couldn't. My wife would take the mattresses out in the yard and take coal oil and saturate them to get rid of bedbugs. And they had an awful time point in bedbugs. But when they got that spray, why, they'd just spray them a little bit over the bed, turn the pillows over and give them a dose. There wasn't any more bedbugs. And it killed the eggs and everything.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, did the IWW strike?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah. Well, they didn't pull a strike, but they would have. They... The company was against them. And they didn't get the pull a strike. I guess they did down on the Palouse.

speaker: John Sanderson or Unknown Speakers
words: Did they have one time when the sparks didn't run?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: They struck on the Potlatch. One of the homes where it took over the Potlatch, it logged in Palouse. T.P. said he was going up to camp one day with a buggy. One of them little buggies. What do you call them? They... It wasn't a hack. I found one of them. Yes, sir. Two horse buggy, but it didn't have no top.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Yeah, I know what you're talking about.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: And Mrs. Jones was with him, and he was going up to camp. There's a big lumberjack that swung out and took the horses by the bits. And Jones said he heard somebody say, Take your hand off of those horses and get away. And he turned around and his wife had a gun on them. And the fellow that blew the horses and backed away. But he said that I made up my mind that I wasn't going to have her alone. I might have trouble. Of course she juked. She sounds like a pretty tough lady. Yeah, she meant business. She meant business. See, that fellow that let loose of them horses, or he'd got it. They sounded like she was a little tougher than him, maybe. Yeah. He's been a head duck, I think. But she had nerve. Jimmy Costello, he... Them old lumberjacks, they was pretty rough in their talk sometimes. He was playing cards up to T.P. Jones. And Mr. Jones was in there. Costello, he got a bad hand. He saw that he was going to get the worst of it. And he said, Fuck such a hand as this. Then he knew what he'd said. Mr. Jones was standing there. Well, he never would go back to T.P.s again.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Mrs. Jones kind of laughed and told T.P.s he didn't need to stay away on that account. She says, I know that they don't lumberjacks get mad and say things that they don't intend to. And he says, I wouldn't hold it against him. But he never went around with his own chap to come.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: He was really... He felt that embarrassed about it. I guess you just wouldn't talk like that around a lady.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: He'd come out before he thought.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I heard Pat used to swear up and down all the time. I heard it was real tough for Pat to keep those swear words out of his mouth.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, probably was. Young Dave Ellison, he practically raised young Dave. They had Ellison's dad, him as a baby, and old Pat was. He liked to take care of young Dave. Young Dave was up here to the picnic. I saw him. Dave told me that if Pat used to let him smoke his pipe when he was five or six, he'd give him a few pups on it. Yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: What about that..… did you hear about that fire at the Verdon place, Gus Verdon?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah. Well, you see, T.P. didn't like Gus Verdon. And when the fire broke out, T.P. was there with the crew. And he directed the hose so that it didn't put the fire out. Verdon was pretty mad about it.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, was there a reason he didn't like Verdon? Because Verdon was a sympathizer with the IWWs?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, something like that. That's what I heard. Mrs. Jones took a little blood and fertilized her flower garden. And the dogs got into it and dug. And she laid it onto the IWW digging it up. They told her that it was his dog's attendant because she put blood in there.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Yeah, it sounds like they used to say the IWWs did a whole lot of things that they didn't do. Yeah, they did.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: They laid everything that they could to tell on to them. But they didn't do nothing.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Why did the company... Why did they hate them so much?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Well, they were going to pull a strike. And... They didn't want no strike.

speaker: John Sanderson or Unknown Speakers
words: I didn't want for one of them. We were in about two weeks from Milwaukee. We were back on the dumb I.M. No, they didn't want a strike. So you guys had to go with us. That's why I told them they'd go. They looked on us nearly, I don't know. But I think about two weeks from the crash, they had to go with us. So they don't want to get in there. We couldn't look for them anymore. So they said they'd push a strike. So they said we got back. Well, they went into the Mayans up around Coeur d 'Alene. They called it several strikes. Yeah, and then they said they were supposed to kneel it for... I don't know. That might have been one of them.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, when I was up in Coeur d 'Alene, that was before it happened out here, wasn't it?

speaker: John Sanderson or Unknown Speakers
words: Yeah. That was even earlier on. Yeah, earlier. We went with Neely and couldn't go back. They said you guys were on a strike. So it was Neely. We went up with Neely and looked on there on the Milwaukee. Checked them before they got the thing. Then we went to Hood. They went several, then we went back on the strike. I remember that. I got a picture of that too, gang. A lot of our men welcome up and look with Neely. That's what they did there. They checked them, I guess, the whole time.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: You know, was that a long time in fact?

speaker: John Sanderson or Unknown Speakers
words: Yeah, the long time back. I forgot when it was.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah… axle up there. Well, the Marion down below, one of the Mayans. The ribs down below were broke, and you couldn't weld it when they were working. John wouldn't allow them to put any overtime on it because it was time and a half. When he took his vacation with Axle footballers and poorly down there every night to weld and fix it up. He said, you know Axle, John Zegler and the guy like this time and a half is going in. When he comes home, made Axle mad. Axle looked up, he said, what did you say? He said, John Zegler and the guy like all this time and a half. Time is going in. He said, who was John Zegler? He looked him right in the face… yeah… what was his name I said… kirk… oh, I forget… he was up here to the picnic, big fella, come up and talk to me. And he looked at him and he said, who was John Zegler?

speaker: John Sanderson
words: He saw that the actor was mad and he turned and left. He didn't say no more. And Axle didn't want anybody but men on his business. He'd run things the way he wanted to. They didn't like it where they could say so. That didn't change him.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I've heard he was really a good farmer. And he knew how to run things.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: He was running Avery. And he had the mechanics working nights to get the bulldozers ready to skid in the morning. Billings from Potlatch, he went up there and he says, Axle, can't you cut out some of this overtime at night? Axle says, yeah. But he says, Mr. Billings, it's wrong if you want it. Well, yes, that's what we got you here for. Well, he says, if them cats are tied up in the daytime and the mechanics working on them, how are they going to log and get logs when they're tied up and being worked on? He says, they work on them at night so they can work the next day. And Billings saw the point. Well, he says, Axle, do the best you can. Well, Axle says, that's what I'm doing. It's just the best way I know how. And he says, if we get logs, we've got to get the cats ready at night to go out in the morning. Well, that's all right. He says, go ahead.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: He was good to the men and he was a good foreman. He knew his stuff and knew what he was doing.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: When he was walking, boss, he used to go around to all the different camps and check and see how they were doing. He said he hiked an awful lot.

speaker: John Sanderson
words: Yeah, he used to hike quite a lot. He was up at Elk River for a long time and I brought him down here. When Parker was here, Elk River had to close down and there wasn't a log in much up there for Axle. He was working down here as assistant superintendent.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Well, Johnny, I...
